skills.name: email-marketing
skills.description: When planning, writing, reviewing, or measuring marketing emails or newsletters (value emails, welcome sequences, list growth, deliverability, copywriting).
skills.instructions:
---
name: email-marketing
description: When planning, writing, reviewing, or measuring marketing emails or newsletters (value emails, welcome sequences, list growth, deliverability, copywriting).
---
# Email marketing

Full sourced research lives beside this file:
- [references/strategy-deliverability-research.md](references/strategy-deliverability-research.md) (cadence, list growth, segmentation, deliverability, benchmarks, testing, legal)
- [references/copywriting-research.md](references/copywriting-research.md) (subject, preview, hooks, structure, P.S., plain vs designed, replies)
- [references/design-research.md](references/design-research.md) (layout, type, color and contrast, images, dark mode, accessibility, Gmail clipping)

## Core rules
1. **Strategy:** every email is useful first; one idea per email; one ask. Small sell in every send (the P.S.), give before asking.
2. **Cadence:** a fixed, predictable schedule beats any "best time." Mailchimp's data peaks near 10 AM weekdays, but that is the best time for only ~6-7% of recipients ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/resources/insights-from-mailchimps-send-time-optimization-system/)). Default weekly, same day and time; test the slot. Go more frequent only after a stable quarter.
3. **List growth:** a lead magnet should fully solve one narrow problem and reveal the next one the paid offer solves (Hormozi, [$100M Leads](https://lythrumpress.com.au/chapter/100m-leads-by-alex-hormozi-section-2/)); diagnosis style works best. Collect signups wherever the audience already is (intake forms, QR at desk, site footer, social bio). Referral loops need a real reward ([Morning Brew](https://referralrock.com/blog/morning-brew-referral-program/)). Quality over count.
4. **Segmentation:** tag every contact by role, interest/product, and status (lead, customer, former). Send one core email, vary the P.S. by segment.
5. **Welcome sequence:** automate ~5 emails over ~2 weeks: deliver magnet, proof, how the offer works, a real story (with permission), hand off to the regular send. Human approves each before it goes live.
6. **Deliverability:** SPF, DKIM, DMARC (p=none min) with aligned From domain; one-click unsubscribe honored within 2 days; spam complaints <0.3%, target <0.1% ([Gmail](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126), [Yahoo](https://senders.yahooinc.com/best-practices/)). Send from your own domain, never a free webmail address ([Mailchimp auth](https://mailchimp.com/help/set-up-email-domain-authentication/)). Keep text >20% of the email, real live text not images ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/resources/email-content-for-deliverability/)). Double opt-in on public forms; never buy/scrape/import non-opted lists; drop hard bounces.
7. **Subject:** a plain headline that names the topic and the reader; curiosity only if line one pays it off. ≤60 characters recommended ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/help/create-ab-tests/)). Never misleading (CAN-SPAM). Write 5+ options, pick one. Consistent From name.
8. **Preview text:** always fill it; finish the subject's thought. Blank shows "Hi Name," and wastes the slot.
9. **Body:** open by continuing the subject line. Skeleton: greeting, hook (real moment or plain problem), the tip (what, when, how much), why it works (one sourced line), one line for the secondary reader, sign-off with no ask, P.S., sources. ~150-250 words (house judgment; HubSpot found 300-500 characters had the best click rate, [2014 report](https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hub/53/file-2191769206-pdf/Science_of_Email_Marketing_2014.pdf)). Write for skimmers: first and last lines carry the point. Real stories only.
10. **P.S. / CTA:** the P.S. is the single ask, restates the next step, gives a true reason for now (season, start date; never fake urgency), and scripts the reply (one word). Replies are an engagement signal MPP can't fake.
11. **Design:** simple wins. In every HubSpot A/B test the simpler email won: plain text got 42% more clicks than a GIF version; an image-heavy HTML template got 51% fewer clicks ([HubSpot](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/plain-text-vs-html-emails-data)). Look like a personal letter: white, one font, one image max, few links.
12. **Measurement:** judge by replies and booked outcomes first, clicks second, unsubscribes/complaints as guardrails, net list growth monthly. Opens are only a deliverability alarm: Apple MPP is roughly half or more of tracked opens ([Litmus](https://www.litmus.com/email-client-market-share/), [MPP](https://www.litmus.com/apple-mail-privacy-protection-resources)). Benchmarks (Mailchimp, Dec 2023): all users 35.63% open, 2.62% click, 0.22% unsub ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/resources/email-marketing-benchmarks/)).
13. **Testing:** one variable at a time, up to 3 variations; Mailchimp recommends ≥5,000 contacts per variation ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/help/about-ab-tests/)), so small lists are directional only. Pick winners by clicks/replies, not opens. One test a month: send time, then subject style, then P.S. placement.
14. **Re-engagement:** quarterly, find contacts with no clicks in 6 months, send 2 short "still want these? reply yes" emails, archive non-responders ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/help/re-engage-inactive-subscribers/)).
15. **Legal and minors:** CAN-SPAM needs truthful headers/subjects, a physical address, a working opt-out, opt-outs honored within 10 business days (2 days for Gmail/Yahoo in practice) ([FTC](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business)). Unchecked opt-in boxes with recorded consent; customers aren't auto-subscribed. COPPA: verifiable parental consent before collecting a child under 13's email; amended rule compliance by April 22, 2026 ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-312)). Collect parent emails for under-13s; written permission before naming or showing a minor. Not legal advice.

## Design (from design research)
- Single 600px column on a white background. Keep it simple and letter-like.
- Body copy is live web-safe text (Helvetica/Arial), 16px, line height 1.5, dark gray (e.g. #222222). Brand fonts only inside images.
- Images go on solid backgrounds, not transparent ones, so logos hold up in dark mode. Always fill in alt text, and repeat any key tip from an image as live text.
- Accent color only where it passes WCAG AA contrast on white; links are underlined; a button, if used, is HTML and at least 44px tall.
- Small print (Sources, footer) at about 12px in mid gray.
- Keep the HTML well under Gmail's ~102KB clipping limit.
- No sourced image-to-text ratio exists; follow the "mostly live text" rule instead.

## Send timing (from send-time research)
- Consistency beats the perfect slot: same day and time every week builds a reading habit.
- Industry day differences are tiny (Tuesday slightly ahead in Omnisend 2026; Klaviyo weekday open rates within about 0.4 points). Don't over-optimize.
- Judge timing on clicks and replies, never opens: Apple Mail Privacy Protection auto-opens mail on Apple's schedule and inflates open rates.
- Test method: run one slot for 4 weeks, then a second slot for 4 weeks, same content type, keep the winner by clicks and replies.
- Check the business's own history first (Mailchimp /reports, timeseries) before trusting benchmarks.
- Full notes: references/send-time-research.md

## Per-issue checklist
**Strategy and cadence**
- [ ] One idea, useful this month, fits the calendar; going out on the fixed schedule.
- [ ] Source for every claim found; every story, name, number, or reward confirmed by the owner, else cut.
**List and segmentation**
- [ ] Right segment(s); P.S. variant per segment chosen. No non-opted contacts.
**Deliverability**
- [ ] Domain authenticated, sending from own domain, one-click unsubscribe, physical address in footer.
- [ ] Mostly live text, ≤1 image, few links.
**Subject and preview**
- [ ] 5+ subject options, plain headline ≤60 chars, not misleading.
- [ ] Preview text filled, finishes the subject's thought.
**Body**
- [ ] First line continues the subject; ~150-250 words; skimmer gets it from first and last lines.
- [ ] Tip states what, when, how much; one sourced "why" line; one line for the secondary reader.
- [ ] Closing line signs off with no ask; signature correct.
**P.S.**
- [ ] Only ask in the email; true reason for now; one-word scripted reply.
**Design**
- [ ] Simple, letter-like; test send to phone and Gmail; preview line reads well.
**Measurement and testing**
- [ ] After send: log replies, booked outcomes, clicks, unsubscribes, complaints. Ignore opens except as an alarm.
- [ ] At most one A/B variable this month, judged by clicks/replies.
**Legal and minors**
- [ ] Opt-out works; address present; no minor named/shown without written permission; under-13 contacts are parent emails only.

## Business-specific notes (Achieve Sports Performance)
- Signature (Ryne 2026-10-14): "Thanks," then "Ryne Gioviano, MSEd, CSCS" then "Achieve Sports Performance & Personal Training".
- Footer (Ryne 2026-10-14): "Achieve Sports Performance & Personal Training", street address, link to www.achievesportsperformance.com, unsubscribe.
- Template: every Achieve Minute starts from templates/achieve-minute.html (copy also at /workspace/newsletter/Achieve-Minute-TEMPLATE.html). Same hosted header image, layout, colors, signature, P.S., Sources and footer; only fill the {{placeholders}}. Do not redesign per issue.
- Send time: primary Tuesday 7:30 AM CT, test Sunday 7:00 PM CT (4 weeks each). Optional Thursday evening for meet/game-weekend issues. Own data (2023 to 2026): morning and Sunday sends had the best median click rates; readers show a second bump around 10 to 11 PM CT; real (non-Apple) opens about 16% to 31%, clicks about 0.6% to 1.6%. Sending domain achieve-personaltraining.com is already authenticated (DKIM, SPF, DMARC p=none).
- No prices in any email. No em dashes anywhere. Never use the word "complimentary"; call it an "evaluation" or "20-minute screen."
- Write to the parent first, plus one "Tell your athlete: ..." line.
- The P.S. is the only ask; it rotates with the season (referral P.S. only once a real reward is supplied). Owner approves every draft before it sends.

# Email Copywriting Research Brief, applied to The Achieve Minute

Prepared for Ryne Gioviano, Achieve Sports Performance, Aurora IL. Date: October 14, 2026.
Scope: subject lines, preview text, opening hooks, structure, length, story vs tips, CTA and P.S., plain text vs designed, voice for parents vs athletes, and driving replies. Every number below names its source. Anything that could not be verified is marked **UNVERIFIED** and is not used as a rule.

---

## Part 1. What the sources say

### 1.1 Measurement first: open rates are noisy
- Mailchimp benchmarks (last updated December 2023, campaigns to 1,000 or more subscribers): all-user average open rate 35.63%, click rate 2.62%, unsubscribe rate 0.22%. Health and fitness: 37.07% opens, 1.87% clicks. Source: Mailchimp, https://mailchimp.com/resources/email-marketing-benchmarks/ and the Mailchimp benchmark PDF linked from that page.
- A "Sports" category at 41.84% opens and 2.88% clicks is attributed to Mailchimp by a secondary site (wethrift.com). I did not see it on the Mailchimp page itself, so treat it as **UNVERIFIED** at the primary source.
- Litmus Email Client Market Share (2026 page): Apple Mail, including Mail Privacy Protection (MPP), shows 62.26% of tracked opens, and Litmus states MPP affects roughly 55 to 60% of all opens. Apple and Gmail together are close to 90% of opens. Source: https://www.litmus.com/email-client-market-share/
- Litmus explains that MPP pre-fetches email content, so Apple Mail users can look like they opened when they did not. Source: https://www.litmus.com/blog/identifying-real-opens-mail-privacy-protection
- **What this means:** do not judge an issue by its open rate. Judge it by replies, clicks, and booked evaluations.

### 1.2 Plain text vs designed
- HubSpot A/B tests: "In every single A/B test, the simpler-designed email won," with statistical significance. Plain text vs a GIF version: plain text got 42% more clicks. Plain text vs an HTML template with images: the HTML version got 51% fewer clicks. A simple HTML template vs a heavy one: the simple one got 30% more clicks. Source: HubSpot, https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/plain-text-vs-html-emails-data
- HubSpot, Science of Email Marketing (2014): nearly two thirds of surveyed professionals said they *preferred* image-based or HTML email, yet in observed data click rate fell as the number of images went up, with close to a one-point drop from zero images to one. In the same report, emails with 300 to 500 characters of body text had the highest click rates in that dataset. Source: https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hub/53/file-2191769206-pdf/Science_of_Email_Marketing_2014.pdf
- Caveat: these are HubSpot's lists and B2B-leaning audiences, and the 300 to 500 character finding is about clicks on a link, not replies or reading. It is a direction, not a law.
- Gary Halbert, *The Boron Letters* (local copy, /workspace/books/classic-sales-marketing/Boron-Letters-Halbert.md): people sort mail into an "A-pile" of letters that look personal and a "B-pile" of things that look like advertising. The A-pile gets read. This is the old-mail version of the HubSpot finding.
- **What this means:** the current format (white background, Helvetica, no heavy template) is right. Keep it looking like a note from Ryne, with one image at most.

### 1.3 Subject lines and preview text
- Halbert (Boron Letters, local copy): the "attention grabber" must be relevant and tie to the message. Attention that does not connect to the body wastes the reader.
- Local file copywriter-master-copy-insights.md (Hopkins, Halbert, Shaw notes): treat the subject line as a headline, say plainly who it is for and what they get, call out the exact reader, and avoid clever "blind" lines that draw the wrong readers. Curiosity is fine only if the first body line pays it off.
- Local file copywriter-new-books-insights.md (Collier, Haldeman-Julius, Shaw notes): proven title forms are "How to...", "Facts you should know about...", and "What X should mean to you."
- Eugene Schwartz, *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966): match the message to the reader's state of awareness (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware). A parent list that already knows the gym is mostly product aware, so the subject line can name the topic directly instead of hiding it.
- Specific numeric claims often repeated online (for example "subject lines under X characters get Y% more opens", or "preview text lifts opens by Z%") could not be tied to a primary source in this pass. **UNVERIFIED**, not used.
- Preview text: Mailchimp lets you set it (the "preview text" field in the campaign builder). If it is left blank, most inboxes show the first line of the body, which for us is "Hi Name," and wastes the space. That behavior is standard, but I have no verified lift figure.
- MPP (Litmus, above) makes open-rate subject line tests unreliable for Apple users. If testing subject lines, judge on clicks or replies.

### 1.4 Opening hooks
- Local master-copy file (Atkinson): the first line after the headline decides whether they keep reading. Sequence is attention, first impression, curiosity, interest.
- Local master-copy file (Hopkins, Letter Writing): continue the line that created the interest. The first sentence should pick up exactly where the subject line left off.
- Hormozi notes (local /workspace/hormozi-advice-videos/COPY.md): get to the meat on the first screen, and lead with proof so the promise is believable.

### 1.5 Structure and length
- Robert Collier (local new-books file): a letter has six parts: an opening that fits the reader's train of thought, a picture, the reason why, proof, a reason to act now, and a close that says exactly what to do. Skimmers read the first paragraph and the last, so the last one must carry the ask.
- Shaw (local files): write for three readers: the one who reads subject plus last line, the skimmer, and the word-by-word reader. Each should get the point.
- HubSpot 2014 (above): 300 to 500 characters of text correlated with the best click rate in its data. For a teaching newsletter the job is reading and replying, not one click, so a short tip of roughly 150 to 250 words is a reasonable house target. That word range is a judgment call, not a sourced figure.

### 1.6 Story vs tips
- Ben Settle (daily email practitioner, author of the *Email Players* newsletter): argues for "infotainment," meaning useful content wrapped in personality or story, sent consistently, so readers look forward to it. This is his practitioner view, not a measured study.
- Hormozi notes (local COPY.md): stories that changed behavior beat "6 tips." State the facts and emphasize, do not manufacture.
- Local master-copy file: story emails use real stories only, with permission.
- **What this means:** one tip per issue, opened with a short real moment from the gym when one exists. No invented athletes.

### 1.7 CTA and P.S.
- Local master-copy file (Halbert): the P.S. restates the next step; it is not a second, different pitch.
- Collier (local): skimmers jump to the end, so the end carries the ask. The P.S. is the most-read spot near the end of a letter. This is copywriting tradition; I found no current primary study with a P.S. readership number, so any percentage you see quoted is **UNVERIFIED**.
- Hopkins via local file: give a true reason to act now (a season date, a block start). Never "limited time" with no reason.
- One ask per email. Maya and Ryne already set this: the closing line signs off and the P.S. is the only ask.

### 1.8 Driving replies
- Local files (Shaw, master copy): script the reply. Tell them exactly what to send, such as one word or "grade, sport, and two after-school times," and remove the last excuse if it is true.
- Local master-copy file: make the action physical and small ("Reply YES").
- Replies also help: a reply is a real engagement signal that MPP cannot fake. That is a reasoned point, not a sourced figure.

### 1.9 Voice for parents vs athletes
- Schwartz awareness levels (above) and Halbert's call-out rule: write to one reader. For this list that reader is the parent.
- Parent wants: is this safe, is it worth the time, will it help my kid's skill and confidence. Athlete wants: what do I do, and how will I feel it in the water or on the field. Write the tip to the parent and include one line the parent can hand to the athlete ("Tell your swimmer: ...").
- Hormozi notes: truth over costume. No hype words.

---

## Part 2. Applied to The Achieve Minute

### 2.1 House rules (locked)
- Mailchimp, white background, Helvetica body.
- Greeting: Hi *|FNAME|*,
- One tip per issue. Mostly for parents, athletes second.
- No prices. No dashes used as long pauses; use periods, commas, and parentheses.
- Call the intake a "20-minute screen" or an "evaluation." Never use the banned intake words or the banned hype words in the brand lock.
- Youth copy covers skill, confidence, and readiness only. No body talk, no timelines, no cure claims.
- Name Aurora in every issue.
- Nothing invented: no names, schools, times, results, or rewards without Ryne.
- The closing line signs off. The P.S. is the single ask and rotates with the calendar. Issue 1 carries the dryland P.S.
- Sign-off: Thanks, Ryne Gioviano, CSCS, Achieve Sports Performance
- Sources in small gray Helvetica under the signature.

### 2.2 Subject line and preview text
- Write the subject as a plain headline for a parent: name the topic and the athlete. Examples of the form (topics must match the real tip): "What your swimmer should drink on meet day" or "How to warm up between events." Avoid teasers the first line does not pay off.
- Always fill Mailchimp's preview text field. Use it to finish the subject's thought, for example "One thing to pack in the bag before Saturday." Never leave it blank, or inboxes show "Hi Name,".
- Write 5 or more subject options per issue and pick one. If Mailchimp A/B testing is used, judge the winner on clicks or replies, not opens (Litmus MPP data).

### 2.3 Body skeleton (about 150 to 250 words)
1. Hi *|FNAME|*,
2. Hook: one or two sentences that pick up the subject line. A real moment from the gym in Aurora, or the plain problem the parent sees.
3. The tip: what to do, when, and how much, in plain sentences.
4. Why it works: one or two sentences, tied to a cited source.
5. The athlete line: "Tell your athlete: ..." in one sentence.
6. Sign-off sentence (no ask), then: Thanks, Ryne Gioviano, CSCS, Achieve Sports Performance
7. P.S. (the only ask)
8. Sources, small gray Helvetica.

### 2.4 P.S. rotation
- Issue 1 (dryland, ahead of the November swimmer push starting Nov 14): P.S. High school swim season is wrapping up. Athletes who start dryland now get the most off-season weeks before club season. Reply "dryland" and we'll set up their evaluation.
- Referral P.S.: runs only once Ryne supplies the real reward. Draft: P.S. Know a teammate who'd want this plan? Forward this email. If they sign up, you both get [reward from Ryne].
- Future slots (each needs Ryne's real dates and details): tryout or season-start readiness, a named program block with its real start date.
- Every P.S. should give a true reason for now and a one-word reply.

### 2.5 Measuring an issue
- Primary: replies to the P.S. keyword and evaluations booked from them.
- Secondary: clicks and unsubscribes (Mailchimp all-user unsubscribe benchmark is 0.22%, Mailchimp page above).
- Ignore open rate as a success measure because of MPP (Litmus).

---

# Email Design Research for The Achieve Minute

Researched 2026-10-14. Every figure below was read in the linked source. Where a source gave no number, none is given here.

## 1. Layout and width
- Mailchimp: "Set email width to 600px or less. Most people view messages in their preview panes, which are narrow and small." Its templates are "never more than 600 pixels wide, or they're fluid-width." https://mailchimp.com/help/about-html-email/
- Mailchimp templates are "designed to be no greater than 600px wide." https://mailchimp.com/help/about-template-widths/
- Mailchimp's HTML email basics: 600 to 800px maximum, "Design for simplicity," avoid floats/positioning, and do not build an email that is "one large, sliced-up image." https://templates.mailchimp.com/getting-started/html-email-basics/
- Takeaway: one single column, 600px max, fluid on phones.

## 2. Mobile and responsive
- Mailchimp: use media queries to increase text size on small screens and give links "thumb-sized (~46x46px) hit areas." https://templates.mailchimp.com/getting-started/html-email-basics/
- Mailchimp accessibility guide: buttons "at least 44 by 44 pixels" with space around them. https://mailchimp.com/resources/accessibility-in-email-marketing/
- WCAG 2.2 Target Size (Minimum) SC 2.5.8 sets 24x24 CSS px as the AA floor; 44x44 is the stronger AAA (2.5.5) target. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html

## 3. Dark mode
- Litmus: optimize logos for both modes, use transparent PNGs, and "add a slight white shadow to images with dark text to keep them readable in Dark Mode." Use high-contrast text/background so partial and full color inverts stay readable. https://www.litmus.com/blog/new-in-litmus-extended-dark-mode-testing
- Litmus developer tips: design with midtones, use a glow or stroke, or put the logo on a shape/background; add `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` styles and duplicate for Outlook with `[data-ogsc]`/`[data-ogsb]`. https://www.litmus.com/blog/coding-emails-for-dark-mode
- Litmus: dark-mode meta tags must be included or the media queries have no effect; image swap mostly works in Apple Mail clients (and Outlook.com only with linked images). https://www.litmus.com/blog/ama-email-developer-tips
- Full guide: https://www.litmus.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-dark-mode-for-email-marketers

## 4. Images and alt text
- Mailchimp: "Assume images will be initially blocked." Use absolute image URLs on a reliable host. https://templates.mailchimp.com/getting-started/html-email-basics/
- Mailchimp alt text: keep it to 1 or 2 sentences, do not repeat captions, mark purely decorative images, and test with images off. https://mailchimp.com/help/add-alt-text-to-images/
- Mailchimp accessibility: keep alt text "under 150 characters"; "Important information should always be in actual text, not embedded in graphics." https://mailchimp.com/resources/accessibility-in-email-marketing/

## 5. Image-to-text ratio
- I found no authoritative source in this pass that publishes a specific ratio, so none is cited. The sourced principle: do not send an all-image email (Mailchimp basics link above) and keep key info in live text (Mailchimp accessibility link above).
- HubSpot's analysis of over half a billion customer emails found even a single image reduced click rate. https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/plain-text-vs-html-emails-data

## 6. Fonts and fallbacks
- Webmail clients strip head/body tags in some cases; Mailchimp advises inline CSS. https://mailchimp.com/help/about-html-email/
- Litmus's own production code uses a stack ending in `Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif`. https://www.litmus.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-dark-mode-for-email-marketers
- Mailchimp accessibility: body text "at least 14 pixels"; avoid all caps beyond short headings. https://mailchimp.com/resources/accessibility-in-email-marketing/
- Inter is not installed on most recipients' devices, so it lives only inside images (header and card). Body is live text in `Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif`.

## 7. Color, contrast, accessibility
- WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum, AA): 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18pt, or 14pt bold). https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html
- WCAG SC 1.4.1 Use of Color: do not rely on color alone to identify links. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html
- Mailchimp: avoid "click here" link text; use descriptive links. https://mailchimp.com/resources/accessibility-in-email-marketing/

Computed contrast (WCAG relative luminance formula, run 2026-10-14):
| Pair | Ratio | AA normal text (4.5) |
|---|---|---|
| #c82536 on #ffffff | 5.56:1 | Pass |
| #ffffff on #c82536 | 5.56:1 | Pass |
| #222222 on #ffffff | 15.91:1 | Pass |
| #333333 on #ffffff | 12.63:1 | Pass |
| #666666 on #ffffff | 5.74:1 | Pass |
| #c82536 on #121212 (dark mode) | 3.37:1 | Fails normal, passes large only |

## 8. Buttons vs text links
- Campaign Monitor: a CTA button instead of a text link gave them "a 28% increase in click-throughs" (their own test). Image buttons are risky because many clients block images. https://www.campaignmonitor.com/email/use-buttons-in-email-campaigns/
- Bulletproof buttons are HTML/CSS (VML for Outlook) with live text. https://www.emailonacid.com/blog/article/email-development/how-to-make-your-emails-bulletproof/ and generator https://www.buttons.cm/

## 9. Gmail clipping
- Gmail clips HTML over 102 KB (102,000 bytes) and shows "View entire message." Hosted image file size does not count; the code does. https://docs.aweber.com/message-editors/messages/why-is-my-message-clipped-in-gmail
- Clipping can hide the unsubscribe link and tracking pixel. https://help.activecampaign.com/hc/en-us/articles/115001060524-Why-is-Gmail-clipping-my-email
- Klaviyo: mobile limits can be lower, around 20 KB on iOS (applied inconsistently) and around 75 KB on other mobile devices. https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/115000591251
- A one-tip email is far below this; just avoid pasting bloated code.

## 10. Mailchimp tips
- Width cannot be changed in the builder; wider than 600px needs custom code. https://mailchimp.com/help/about-template-widths/
- Merge tags such as `*|FNAME|*` personalize; set a default value for missing names. https://mailchimp.com/help/getting-started-with-merge-tags/ and https://mailchimp.com/help/all-the-merge-tags-cheat-sheet/
- Preview text: set it in the campaign field; in custom code use `*|MC_PREVIEW_TEXT|*`. https://mailchimp.com/help/edit-your-emails-subject-preview-text-from-name-or-from-email-address/
- Test with live merge tag info or a small live segment; normal tests do not fill contact merge tags. https://mailchimp.com/help/preview-and-test-your-email-campaign/
- Recommendation: the drag-and-drop builder is enough (Image, Text, Button blocks). No custom code needed.

## 11. Plain text vs designed: evidence
- HubSpot A/B tests: plain text beat a GIF version with 42% more clicks; an HTML template with images got 51% fewer clicks than plain text; a simple HTML template beat an HTML-heavy one with 30% more clicks. https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/plain-text-vs-html-emails-data
- HubSpot 2014 survey: 64% said they prefer HTML emails; 79% of ages 30 to 44 vs 49% of those over 60. Stated preference and observed clicks disagree. https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hub/53/file-2191769206-pdf/Science_of_Email_Marketing_2014.pdf
- Litmus test: plain text style won with customers, but they note the first test was flawed (messaging differed too); for non-customers format did not seem to matter. https://www.litmus.com/blog/the-results-are-in-a-b-testing-html-vs-plain-text-emails
- Takeaway: light design, mostly live text, few images. That is exactly "simple, professional."

---

## Applied to The Achieve Minute

**Structure (single column, top to bottom)**
1. Preview text (40 to 90 chars, the tip's payoff).
2. Header image, Achieve-Minute-Header.png, displayed 600x150 (file is 1200x300, so 2x for retina).
3. Hi *|FNAME|*, plus a 1 to 2 sentence intro in live text.
4. Tip card image, 1080x1350, displayed 600x750 (or 480 wide centered if it feels tall).
5. The same tip repeated in live text below the card (3 short lines plus the one rule), so it works with images off and for screen readers.
6. Optional single bulletproof button, only if there is a link.
7. Thanks, Ryne signature.
8. P.S. plug.
9. Sources block.
10. Mailchimp footer (address, unsubscribe).

**Specs**
- Container 600px max, fluid 100% under 600px. Background #ffffff.
- Side padding 24px desktop, 16px mobile. 24px between blocks.
- Body: `font-family: Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;` 16px, line-height 1.5 (24px), color #222222 (15.91:1).
- Headings in live text (if any): 22 to 24px bold, #111111, line-height 1.25.
- Links: #c82536 and underlined (5.56:1 passes AA; underline satisfies use-of-color).
- Button: #c82536 fill, #ffffff 16px bold text (5.56:1), min 44px tall, padding 14px 28px, radius 4px, HTML not image.
- P.S.: 16px, "P.S." in bold.
- Sources: 12px, line-height 1.5, #666666 (5.74:1), top border 1px #e5e5e5, padding-top 16px. Mailchimp's 14px minimum is for body text; this is small reference text, raise to 13 to 14px if you want strict.
- Images: always set width/height attributes and `style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto;"`, hosted in Mailchimp.

**Alt text examples**
- Header: `The Achieve Minute from Achieve Sports Performance`
- Card: `Game day fueling: real breakfast 3 to 4 hours out, small snack 60 to 90 minutes out, carbs plus protein within an hour after. One rule: nothing new on game day.` (under 150 chars is ideal; trim if Mailchimp cuts it)

**Dark mode**
- Header and card are white-background PNGs, so in dark mode they show as bright white rectangles. That is acceptable and reads as a "card." Do not make them transparent: the charcoal logo text would vanish on dark backgrounds.
- If we ever use a transparent logo, add a subtle white stroke or glow per Litmus, or keep it on a white plate.
- The red #c82536 drops to 3.37:1 on near-black, so if a client inverts the body, red links are only large-text safe. Keep links underlined so they stay identifiable.
- Mailchimp drag-and-drop does not need custom dark-mode code. Test in Gmail app and Apple Mail dark mode before the first send.

**Size**
- Two images plus short text sits well under Gmail's 102 KB clip limit. Avoid pasting from Google Docs/Word (adds code bloat).

**Do not**
- Put the tip only in the image. Use "click here." Add more than 2 images. Use Inter as live text.

# Achieve Minute: Best Send Day and Time (research, Oct 14 2026)

## Recommendation
- **Primary: Tuesday, 7:30 AM CT.** It's a weekday morning and fits the parent routine before drop-off. Tuesday was the best day for opens and clicks in Omnisend's 2026 data. In Ryne's own history, morning sends had the highest median click rate.
- **Backup / test: Sunday, 7:00 PM CT.** That's when families plan the week. Sunday sends had Ryne's highest median click rate, but there were only 5 of them.
- **How to decide:** run each slot for 4 weeks and keep the same time every week. Judge on **clicks and replies, not opens**, because Apple Mail Privacy Protection makes open counts and open times unreliable. Keep the winner.
- **Content timing:** for meet- or game-related issues, a Thursday evening send can land closer to the weekend. That's optional, and only for topical issues.

## Ryne's own Mailchimp data (All Subscribers, read-only)
- 217 campaign reports exist. The monthly newsletter has gone to All Subscribers since 2020. The list now has about 1,150 to 1,190 recipients per send.
- Recent reported open rates are 49% to 69%. **With Apple proxy opens excluded,** recent sends drop to 16% to 31%. For example, the Summer 2026 newsletter shows 64.9% reported but 28.9% excluding proxy opens. Clicks are low, about 0.6% to 1.6% per send recently.
- **24-hour open timelines (5 recent sends):**

| Send (CT) | Excl.-proxy open rate | 24h pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Wed 10/08/25 4:10 PM | 30.7% | 320 opens in the first hour, 15 clicks in 24h, small bump at 10 PM |
| Mon 7/6/26 11:19 AM | 28.9% | 338 opens in the first hour, small bump at 10 PM |
| Sat 12/6/25 1:07 PM | 28.8% | 292 in the first hour, 13 clicks |
| Thu 3/5/26 3:50 PM | 19.5% | 125 then 134 in the first two hours, 6 clicks |
| Mon 4/6/26 1:36 PM | 15.7% | 134 in the first hour, 9 clicks |

- **Takeaways:**
  - Most opens and clicks happen within 1 to 2 hours of the send (part of that first-hour spike is Apple prefetch), so the send time itself matters.
  - There is a consistent second, smaller bump around 10 to 11 PM CT. Parents read late.
  - Almost nothing happens from about 1 AM to 7 AM.
- **Median click rate by send day, 2023 to 2026 (41 newsletters):**
  - Sun 2.5% (5 sends), Fri 1.9% (4), Tue 1.8% (8), Wed 1.6% (5), Thu 1.4% (7), Sat 1.4% (7), Mon 1.0% (5)
  - By time of day: morning 1.8% (9), evening 1.9% (8), midday 1.3% (9), late afternoon 1.4% (15)
- **Caveat:** the samples are tiny, and click rates fell over time no matter the day. Sends have never been timed on purpose, so treat this data as a hint, not proof.

## Mailchimp features
- Send Time Optimization (based on clicks) and Timewarp require the Standard plan or higher. The API only reports "monthly" as the plan type. The account has 17 audiences, more than the Essentials (3) or Standard (5) limits, which suggests a legacy plan. Check under Account > Billing.
- Timewarp doesn't matter much here, since nearly everyone is in Central time.

## Industry research
- **Omnisend (2026, ~26B emails):**
  - Tuesday leads for opens (31.3%) and clicks (0.81% click-to-sent). Friday leads for conversions.
  - Best hours: 9 AM for opens, 4 PM for clicks, 7 AM for conversions.
  - https://www.omnisend.com/blog/best-time-to-send-email/
- **Klaviyo (2023 data):**
  - Wednesday and Thursday are best overall. Weekday differences are tiny: open rates run from 12.14% to 12.52% Monday through Friday.
  - https://www.klaviyo.com/blog/best-day-to-send-emails
- **Brevo:**
  - Tuesday and Thursday, 10 AM to 3 PM. Wednesday gets the most clicks. Weekends are weakest.
  - https://www.brevo.com/blog/best-time-to-send-email/
- **MoEngage EU 2025 benchmarks:** no significant difference by send day.
  - https://info.moengage.com/hubfs/EU%20Marketing/EU%20Email%20Benchmarks%20Report%202025.pdf
- **Parent audiences** (weak evidence: vendor blogs from school-communication companies, and they contradict each other):
  - Daystage says Sunday 6 to 9 PM or Monday 7 to 9 AM, and that a consistent send time builds a reading habit. https://www.daystage.com/blog/guides/school-newsletter-open-rates-research
  - Another Daystage piece says Tuesday to Thursday, 7 to 9 AM. https://www.daystage.com/blog/principals/school-newsletter-open-rate
- **Apple Mail Privacy Protection:**
  - Apple preloads emails, so they register as opened even when unread, and open times reflect Apple's prefetch schedule. Use clicks to judge timing.
  - Mailchimp: https://mailchimp.com/help/apple-privacy-faq/
  - Postmark: https://postmarkapp.com/blog/how-apples-mail-privacy-changes-affect-email-open-tracking
  - SendGrid: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/tracking-events/understanding-apple-mail-privacy-protection-and-open-events
- **Mailchimp plan features:**
  - https://mailchimp.com/help/use-send-time-optimization/
  - https://mailchimp.com/help/use-timewarp/


--- file: references/strategy-deliverability-research.md ---
# Email and Newsletter Marketing Research for Achieve Sports Performance
Prepared 2026-10-14. Applies to The Achieve Minute (short value emails with a P.S. plug) and the quarterly newsletter, sent from Mailchimp. Every number below links to its source. Where no source was found, there is no number.

House rules for every recommendation: no prices in emails, no em dashes, never use the word "complimentary", evaluations are offered in the evenings, and Ryne approves every draft before it sends.

## 1. Cadence, frequency, and send timing
- **Mailchimp's send-time research:** Across Mailchimp's whole data set, weekdays do best and about 10 AM local time is the broadest peak. But 10 AM is the best time for only a small share of recipients (about 6 to 7 percent), so there is no single best time. Sources: [Mailchimp send-time insights](https://mailchimp.com/resources/insights-from-mailchimps-send-time-optimization-system/), [analysis of that data](https://jacobfilipp.com/maildata/insights-from-mailchimps-send-time-optimization-system/index.html).
- **Send Time Optimization:** Mailchimp's feature delivers each email within 24 hours of the date you pick, at the time that contact usually engages. It needs the Standard plan or higher, enough engagement history, and scheduling at least 48 hours ahead. Source: [Mailchimp help](https://mailchimp.com/help/use-send-time-optimization/).
- **What the experts do:** Ben Settle sends one short plain-text email every day and sells in every one ([Ben Settle](https://bensettle.com/blog/how-to-make-6-figures-per-year-writing-one-email-per-day/)). Ann Handley's Total Annarchy goes out every two weeks and is personal and built on stories ([Campaign Monitor case study](https://www.campaignmonitor.com/blog/email-marketing/how-ann-handley-grew-her-newsletter/)). What they share is a fixed, predictable schedule. How often you send matters less than sending on schedule.
- **For Achieve:** Send The Achieve Minute once a week, on the same weekday every time. Parents of school-age athletes tend to read in the evening after practice, but that is my guess, not a sourced fact, so test it (section 9). The quarterly newsletter stays separate and goes out at the start of each season: fall, winter, spring, and summer. Don't send daily until the weekly email has held steady for one quarter.

## 2. List growth and lead magnets
- **Hormozi ($100M Leads):** A lead magnet should fully solve one narrow problem and, in doing so, reveal the next problem, which the paid offer solves. He names three types: reveal a problem (a diagnosis), give a sample or trial, or give one step of a multi-step process. Make it good enough that you could charge for it, and end with one clear call to action. Source: [$100M Leads summary](https://lythrumpress.com.au/chapter/100m-leads-by-alex-hormozi-section-2/).
- **Ramit Sethi:** Go for quality subscribers over raw numbers. Solve an urgent pain, promote the lead magnet where the audience already spends time, and make signing up easy. Source: [I Will Teach You To Be Rich](https://www.iwillteachyoutoberich.com/how-to-build-an-email-list/).
- **Morning Brew's referral program:** Referrals are widely reported to have driven a large share of its growth. Second-hand reports put the referral share of growth anywhere from about 30 percent to as high as 80 percent in early periods. Source: [Referral Rock](https://referralrock.com/blog/morning-brew-referral-program/). Their setup used personal referral links and rewards that grew at each milestone.
- **Lead magnet ideas for Achieve (all diagnosis-style, all leading to the eval):** "Swim Dryland Readiness Check" (5 at-home tests a parent can film), "Is Your Athlete's Jump Telling You Something? (what force plates measure)", "In-Season Strength Checklist for HS Athletes". Every one ends with the evening evaluation as the next step.
- **Where to collect signups:** the eval intake form (with a consent checkbox), the front desk QR code, the website footer, Instagram bio, and handouts for team and club parents.

## 3. Segmentation
Set up Mailchimp tags or groups: **Role** (Parent, Athlete 13+, Adult client), **Sport** (Swim, Other), **Status** (Lead, Evaluated, Active, Former). Always segment by role and by swim versus other sports. Send one Achieve Minute to everyone but swap in a segment-specific P.S. (Mailchimp conditional merge tags or separate sends). Leave athletes under 13 off the list entirely (see section 10).

## 4. Welcome and nurture sequence
New subscribers are at their most engaged when they first sign up, so automate a short sequence (Mailchimp Customer Journeys):
1. Day 0: Deliver the lead magnet. Answer first, then give one sentence on who Ryne is.
2. Day 2: The proof: 130 college commits (about 70 percent D1), 6 Olympic Trials qualifiers.
3. Day 5: How the eval works (force plates, then a written program). Evaluations are in the evenings, and the call to action is to reply to book.
4. Day 9: A story about one named athlete, used with permission.
5. Day 14: Hand off to the weekly Achieve Minute.
Every sequence email goes to Ryne for approval before the automation is turned on.

## 5. Deliverability
- **Gmail and Yahoo rules (in force since 2024):** Bulk senders must have SPF, DKIM, and DMARC (p=none at minimum), with the From domain aligned. Marketing email must support one-click unsubscribe, and unsubscribes must be honored within 2 days (48 hours). Keep spam complaints under 0.3 percent, ideally under 0.1 percent. Sources: [Gmail sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126), [Gmail FAQ](https://support.google.com/a/answer/14229414?hl=en), [Yahoo Sender Hub](https://senders.yahooinc.com/best-practices/).
- **Mailchimp setup:** Account & billing > Domains > authenticate achievesportsperformance.com. This adds 2 CNAME records (DKIM) and 1 TXT record (DMARC). Validation can take up to 48 hours. Send from ryne@achievesportsperformance.com, never from a gmail.com address. Source: [Mailchimp domain authentication](https://mailchimp.com/help/set-up-email-domain-authentication/).
- **Plain vs designed, and image-to-text ratio:** Mailchimp advises keeping text above 20 percent of the email and using several content blocks instead of one large image. Source: [Mailchimp content for deliverability](https://mailchimp.com/resources/email-content-for-deliverability/). For Achieve: The Achieve Minute should look like a personal letter, with mostly text, at most one image, and few links. The quarterly newsletter can carry Designer's card, but the key copy should be live text, not baked into the image.
- **List hygiene:** Use double opt-in for public forms. Never import scraped or purchased lists or team rosters that didn't opt in. Remove hard bounces.

## 6. Subject lines and preview text
Mailchimp allows subject lines up to 150 characters but recommends 60 or fewer ([Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/help/create-ab-tests/)). Subject lines that are specific and concrete fit the brand: "The jump test that predicts swim starts." Always write preview text that continues the subject line instead of repeating it. CAN-SPAM bans misleading subject lines ([FTC](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business)). Stick to one consistent From name, for example "Ryne at Achieve".

## 7. Benchmarks (use with caution)
| Source | Category | Open | Click | Unsub |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Mailchimp](https://mailchimp.com/resources/email-marketing-benchmarks/) (data last updated Dec 2023) | Education + Training | 35.64% | 3.02% | 0.18% |
| Mailchimp | All users | 35.63% | 2.62% | 0.22% |
| [SaaS Scored](https://saasscored.com/blog/email-marketing-benchmarks-by-industry), compiling MailerLite/ActiveCampaign/Moosend data | Health & Fitness | 47.81% | 1.45% | 0.29% |
| SaaS Scored | Sports & Recreation | 47.69% | 1.27% | 0.16% |

**Apple MPP:** Apple Mail Privacy Protection loads emails automatically, which records "opens" nobody made. Litmus reports Apple (including MPP) at roughly half of all tracked opens (49.79 percent in March 2025) and says MPP-affected opens can exceed 50 percent of opens. Sources: [Litmus market share](https://www.litmus.com/email-client-market-share/), [Litmus MPP center](https://www.litmus.com/apple-mail-privacy-protection-resources). Treat open rate as a rough trend signal only, useful mainly for spotting a sudden drop that points to a deliverability problem.

## 8. Measuring what matters
Track these each month in a simple sheet:
1. **Replies** per send. The P.S. asks for a reply, so replies are the main signal.
2. **Evaluations booked** that can be traced back to an email (ask "how did you hear" at booking, and use the reply keyword such as "dryland").
3. **Click rate** on the single link.
4. **Unsubscribes and spam complaints** (complaints must stay under 0.1 percent).
5. **List growth** net of unsubscribes.
Opens are tracked only to spot deliverability trends.

## 9. A/B testing in Mailchimp
Mailchimp A/B tests one variable at a time (subject line, From name, content, or send time) with up to 3 variations. The test must go to at least 10 percent of the list, and Mailchimp recommends at least 5,000 contacts per variation for reliable results. Send-time tests go to 100 percent of the list. Multivariate tests allow up to 8 combinations. Sources: [Create A/B test](https://mailchimp.com/help/create-ab-tests/), [About A/B tests](https://mailchimp.com/help/about-ab-tests/), [Multivariate](https://mailchimp.com/help/create-multivariate-tests/).
**For Achieve:** The list is almost certainly far below 5,000 per variation, so treat test results as directional only. Pick winners by clicks, not opens, because MPP inflates opens. Test one thing per month: first send day/time (e.g., Tue 7 PM vs Sun 7 PM CT), then the subject line style, then where the P.S. sits.

## 10. Re-engagement and sunsetting
Mailchimp can find inactive contacts (contact rating or no recent engagement). Send them a re-engagement campaign, then archive those who still don't respond. Archiving removes them from the audience but keeps their data. Sources: [Identify inactive](https://mailchimp.com/help/identify-inactive-subscribers/), [Re-engage](https://mailchimp.com/help/re-engage-inactive-subscribers/), [Archive](https://mailchimp.com/help/remove-inactive-contacts/).
**For Achieve:** Every quarter, find contacts with no clicks for 6 months (judge by clicks, because MPP opens can't be trusted). Send them 2 short emails, for example "Still want these? Reply yes." Archive anyone who doesn't respond. Graduated seniors could move to an adult or alumni segment instead of getting cut.

## 11. Legal
- **CAN-SPAM (FTC):** No false headers or misleading subject lines. Identify the email as an ad where that applies. Include a valid physical address (4020 Fox Valley Center Drive, Aurora, IL). Include a clear opt-out that keeps working for 30 days after sending. Honor opt-outs within 10 business days (Gmail and Yahoo require 2 days, so in practice the deadline is 2 days). Being a member doesn't exempt someone from these protections. Sources: [FTC compliance guide](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business), [FTC 2023 blog](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2023/08/when-sending-commercial-email-businesses-cant-unsubscribe-can-spam-compliance).
- **Consent:** Use an explicit opt-in checkbox, not pre-checked, and keep a record of it (Mailchimp logs signup source and time). Clients aren't on the marketing list automatically just because they are clients.
- **Minors / COPPA:** COPPA generally requires verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information, including an email address, from a child under 13. The amended rule took effect June 23, 2025, with compliance required by April 22, 2026. Sources: [eCFR 16 CFR 312](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-312), [Federal Register 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/22/2025-05904/childrens-online-privacy-protection-rule), [FTC press release](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/01/ftc-finalizes-changes-childrens-privacy-rule-limiting-companies-ability-monetize-kids-data). **For Achieve:** Collect parent emails only for anyone under 13 (athletes start at 11). For athletes 13 to 17, a parent should opt them in or be copied. Get written permission before naming or showing any minor athlete. This is general research, not legal advice; check with counsel.

## 12. Expert frameworks, condensed
- **Hormozi:** Lead magnets that reveal the next problem. Give, give, give, then ask. Source above.
- **Ben Settle:** Send daily, keep it short and in plain text, show personality, and sell in every email. Lesson for Achieve: a small sell in every email, which is what the P.S. does.
- **Ramit Sethi:** Quality list, solve an urgent pain, earn the right to sell.
- **Morning Brew:** Referral loop with personal links and milestone rewards. Lesson for Achieve: the referral P.S. needs a real reward from Ryne.
- **Justin Welsh:** Saturday Solopreneur goes out every week at the same time and has reportedly grown without a referral program ([Newsletter Engines](https://mikeromaine.com/referral-systems-newsletters/)). Lesson: being consistent beats gimmicks.
- **Ann Handley:** Write to one person, tell stories, keep a personal voice. Grew from 0 to 42,000 subscribers ([Campaign Monitor](https://www.campaignmonitor.com/blog/email-marketing/how-ann-handley-grew-her-newsletter/)).
- **Mailchimp / Litmus research:** Authenticate the domain, keep plenty of real text in the email, judge by clicks over opens, and archive inactive contacts.

## 13. Top recommendations for Achieve
1. Authenticate achievesportsperformance.com in Mailchimp (DKIM plus DMARC p=none) and send only from Ryne's gym address before Issue 1 goes out.
2. Send The Achieve Minute weekly on one fixed evening, and keep the quarterly newsletter as a separate seasonal send.
3. Make The Achieve Minute a plain, letter-style email with one idea, one link at most, and the P.S. as the only ask, asking for a reply keyword.
4. Measure replies and booked evening evaluations first, clicks second, and opens only as a deliverability alarm.
5. Tag every contact by role (parent, athlete 13+, adult) and sport (swim vs other), and vary the P.S. by segment.
6. Build one diagnosis-style lead magnet (Swim Dryland Readiness Check) and put the signup on the eval form, front desk QR code, website, and Instagram.
7. Turn on a 5-email welcome sequence that ends with the evening evaluation invite, after Ryne approves each email.
8. Collect parent emails only for athletes under 13, use unchecked opt-in boxes, and get written permission before naming a minor.
9. Every quarter, send a 2-email re-engagement campaign to contacts with no clicks in 6 months, then archive the ones who still don't respond.
10. Run one A/B test a month in Mailchimp (send day first), pick winners by clicks, and treat results as directional at our list size.

skills.instructions:
---
name: Eval cutoffs
description: >-
  Use when deciding Positive vs limited on Achieve eval or PRI battery tests,
  or locking Pos phrasing for program-Asana notes from measured degrees.
---
# Achieve eval Pos cutoffs

Use this when filling program-Asana notes from an Assessment. Prefer the sheet’s own Pos/Neg marks when present. When the sheet only lists degrees (or blank Pos), apply the cutoffs below.

Run the helper for batch checks:
`python3 /home/box/agent-data/shared/scripts/achieve/eval_pos_cutoffs.py --help`

## Ryne-locked degree cutoffs (2026-11-03)
These three override the “no absolute cutoff” PRI gap for Achieve Pos phrasing:
- **FA IR:** <45° = Pos
- **FA ER:** <50° = Pos
- **HG ER:** <90° = Pos

(AAOS/textbook-style house rules. PT measured seated norms for FA IR/ER are closer to ~33-38°; still use these locked thresholds for Pos.)

## PRI manual degree cutoffs (Pos = limited)
- **Passive SLR / Passive leg raise:** <75° limited; >100° excessive (both Pos). Sources: Myokinematic SLR; Pelvis Cranial Resolution form `<75° >100°`.
- **PART (Passive Abduction Raise):** <45° abduction. Source: Pelvis PART.
- **HG / Shoulder horizontal abduction:** <45°. Source: Postural Respiration BC tests.
- **HG IR:** <80-90° (use **<85°** as the single house midpoint when a binary is needed; <80 clearly Pos, 80-90 soft zone). Source: Postural Respiration HG IR.
- **Shoulder flexion (HG flexion):** <160°. Source: Postural Respiration Shoulder Flexion.

I&I “SLR at least 70°, not greater than 100°” is treatment-target language; prefer <75° / >100° for Pos/Neg.

## No absolute degree cutoff (Pos by pattern / side-to-side / can’t-do)
- **ADT:** Pos = femur will not adduct. Usually L in Left AIC; bilateral → PEC.
- **EDT:** Pos = tested LE restricted in hip extension / femur does not approach table.
- **PADT:** Neg = top knee to neutral @ 90° knee flex and touches mat; Pos = cannot.
- **Apical expansion:** Pos = cannot fill one apex as easily as the other.
- **Trunk rotation:** Pos = unequal L vs R.
- **Standing reach / toe touch:** Left AIC & PEC >0″ (can’t touch); Patho PEC 0″ with +B ADT/+B PADT.
- **Functional Squat:** Left AIC/PEC <3/5; Patho PEC >3/5.
- **ISA Wide vs Narrow:** Achieve labeling only - no PRI ° cutoff.
- **Back To Wall Flexion:** no printed cutoff; Pos when sheet says limited / can’t.

## Pattern matrices (Pelvis)
- Left AIC: +L ADT, Standing Reach >0″, +L PADT, +R PART, Functional Squat <3/5
- PEC: +B ADT, Standing Reach >0″, +B PADT, PART − bilat, Functional Squat <3/5
- Patho PEC: +B ADT, Standing Reach 0″, +B PADT, PART + uni/bilat, Functional Squat >3/5

## Achieve Assessment sheet
Template "Assessment Template 2023" prints no degree Pos/Neg cutoffs for these tests (blank R/L/Comments). Printed sheet criteria only: Beighton Hypermobile >3; Clavicular Angle 6°-20°.

## Asana Pos phrasing
Prefer sheet language (`Pos B FA IR`, `Pos toe touch - can't reach`). When degrees drive the call:
- `Pos R FA IR` / `Pos B FA IR` etc. when under cutoff on that side
- Include the degree in notes only when it helps (`R FA ER 55 vs L 65`) - still mark Pos if under cutoff

---
# Exercise progressions and selections

Source CSV (authoritative ladder):  
`/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/exercise-progressions.csv`

Columns: `Exercise Name`, `Exercise Category`, `YouTube Link`, `Intent`, `Exercise Level` (Beginner / Intermediate / Advanced), `Advanced Eligible?`, `Equipment Needed`, `Variables`, `Regression`, `Alternative`, `Exercise Instructions`.

## How to use
1. Pick the **category** the slot needs.
2. Open that category skill below (or filter the CSV).
3. Match **level**, **equipment**, and **Intent**.
4. Start at the default. Fail → **Regression**. Same-level swap → **Alternative**.
